abstract: Mitotic spindle function depends on multiple forces that are difficult to measure in cells. In fission yeast, the spindle assembles and elongates within an intact nuclear envelope. Without the kinesin-14/Pkl1, spindle microtubule minus ends detach from the spindle pole body and are pushed beyond it by kinesin-5/Cut7 sliding, forming protrusions that deform the nuclear envelope. We quantified and modeled protrusion dynamics. We found that as protrusions grew, the spindle often shortened, and the extent of shortening correlated with loss of spindle Cut7. Cells with protrusions showed a delay in anaphase onset. A force-balance model can explain fast and slow protrusion length changes, and inferred overlap length at force balance estimated the midzone sliding force density. After laser ablation, severed protrusions retracted and stopped near the cut, consistent with nuclear envelope-driven sliding. The results show the importance of minus-end anchoring for spindle mechanics and how protrusions can probe mechanical coupling between the spindle and nuclear envelope.

summary: In fission yeast lacking kinesin-14 Pkl1, spindle microtubule minus-end protrusions perturb force balance, shorten spindles and delay anaphase onset.
